utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Waespi, I had forgotten yesterday to come back to your -- well, announcement or request. It was not entirely clear to me that you intended to file the report, which I would then take would be a confidential filing. I have not checked this morning whether you have done it already. But there is no --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, I left it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We also have it uploaded in the e-court system so we could release it under seal, or whatever you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is happy if you would file it, but then, of course, confidentially. That seems to be a better approach than to just release it in the e-court. If there is no other procedural matter, then, Mr. Kay, is the Cermak Defence ready to call its next witness, which I do understand no protective measures and that would be Branko Sruk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, Could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. There was an issue about a relatively late filing of this witness. Mr. Waespi, the 92 ter statement was filed relatively late. I'm not saying too late. But is there anything to be expected in terms of -- yes, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that problem doesn't exist anymore. Now, perhaps we could also already try to use our time. There are two documents. The first being a compilation of documents which the Cermak Defence would like to have added to its 65 ter list. Mr. Carrier, that's the compilation of documents on sanitation from August 1995 and an order on disbanding mixed detachments for sanitation and transferring sanitation to civilian organs, 4th of September. Any problem with adding it to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sruk. Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text will now be handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sruk. Please be seated. Mr. Sruk, you will first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sruk. Mr. Sruk, there is going to be a document that will come on the screen to the right of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have 2D00765.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it is your witness statement that you gave to the Defence. And I ask you to look at it to identify it. Can you see there the statement that you gave to the Defence, when you were interviewed on the 10th of September, 2009. And if the page can be brought down a bit, do you identify your signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we could just turn to the last page of the document, which has the date, 7th of October, 2009, do you confirm that is your signature and you signed this document on that date?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: That's correct. Everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the pages in between are signed by the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, I'm going to ask you some questions about this statement. First of all, when you signed this document, did you read through its contents?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes, twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you read it, was everything contained in the statement, to the best of your knowledge and belief, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: In my statement, is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if I was to ask you in court today the same questions you were asked and in which the information was recorded in this statement, would you give the same answers to those questions so that the answers remained the same?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes. These are the only possible answers I could give.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sruk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in those circumstances, may I make this document an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1737.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1737 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, we're now just going to complete some formalities in relation to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in paragraph 7, there are two documents referenced with OBR numbers. The first is OBR-068311, which goes to page 14. Those are the two pages that have been cited. This is 2D00766. And I request that that be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1738.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1738 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, at line 21 in the same paragraph is a similar document identified OBR-0686. That has been uploaded onto our 65 ter list as 2D00767. I ask that that be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1739.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1739 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes the formalities of the statement. I'll now give a short summary of the contents of that statement. Mr. Sruk, since November 2006, is currently the head of the occupational medicine department in the Sunce Polyclinic. In 1995, he was within the health department of Operations Group North of the Split Military District, and his superior was the commander of Operations Group North and he reported to the chief of the health department at the Split Military District. At that time, he was the commander of a military health care centre. Just before Operation Storm, on the 3rd of August, 1995, he had arranged a hygiene and sanitation reception point with a surgical team in the hamlet of Marici, near the village of Luka, which was located near Sajkovici, where Operation Group's North command post was. Having undertaken his duties there, on the 5th of August, 1995, he received an order from the staff of Operations Group North to go to Knin immediately with all available hygiene and sanitation and -- personnel with the task of organising the reception centre for Croatian Army members. Early on the 6th of August, he went to Knin and he first visited the hospital and situated himself in a building nearby. During the morning of the 6th of August, he went into Knin, as the communications were not functioning, and near the railway station met a group of people wearing HV uniforms. They informed him they had been carrying out human sanitation of the terrain and that they had taken some dead bodies to Knin cemetery. When he heard of this, he went to the cemetery to check what was happening there, and whether things were in accordance with the established rules and protocol. There was no one at the cemetery at that time, but he found a hole containing some dead bodies near the chapel. At that stage, the Croatian military was responsible for the human sanitation in the area of combat activities, the front line, and the civil protection of police administrations was responsible for the human sanitation in the liberated area. He took no action at that stage, knowing that it was their responsibility to deal with matters. He went to the military health care centre, returned to the cemetery later in the day where he found staff of the civilian protection dealing with the burial of bodies within Knin cemetery, according to accepted standards. In relation to issues in this case, Mr. Sruk has considered an order that was titled: I hereby order, dated 5th of August, 1995, Exhibit P506, signed by Mr. Cermak, and concerning a Dr. Brkic. He has considered the information with that order and has identified the fact that it not only names him but also people working for him. And it is his evidence that, in fact, he never did work with Dr. Brkic, and that reports filed by Dr. Brkic record the work of other people which, in his view, he concludes that Dr. Brkic was seeking to identify himself and self-promote himself in relation to having conducted activities in connection with Operation Storm. Your Honour, having given that brief summary of Dr. Sruk's statement, I'll now ask him some questions of clarification, with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dr. Sruk, I want to turn now to when you arrived Knin on the 6th of August. If you could tell the Court what time it was when you arrived the town.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Roughly at dawn, we were near Sinj, so that at around 8.00, 8.30, we were in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where did you visit in Knin, first of all? What place did you go to initially when you arrived Knin?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Pursuant to the verbal order I received, we went immediately to the hospital in Knin. I knew where it was located from before so we found it quite soon. It was our intention to organise there a reception centre and an infirmary for wounded or injured soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you establish at that time the reception centre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: It was a rather makeshift version at the time, which enabled us to, over a short period of time, and we had a team of surgeons and nurses from the nearby area, to put the whole thing together and have it up and running.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was this located within the Knin hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes. It was right next to the main entrance where the emergency ward existed from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At that stage, when you were establishing the reception centre, how many operatives within your -- your unit did you have working with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the composition of this team that you had was what? Nurses, doctors, if you could describe it to us.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: The team was composed of individuals who had previously been in the village of Marici and had been receiving individuals there. During Operation Storm there was a surgeon, an anesthesiologist, nurses, drivers, myself as a doctor, and male nurses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you went into Knin town itself, to the railway station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: As soon as we organised ourselves, I went to get informed, to know what was happening. As you might know, the hospital in Knin is at the edge of town, and we wanted to see what the situation was like in this new environment we came to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what did you establish within the town, which is of relevance to this case?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: In principle, the town was deserted. There were several broken shop windows, and at the railway station, facing the main square of the town of Knin, I came across a group of uniformed individuals, two or three of whom I recognised because we were members of the same unit back in 1991. As there was a general celebratory mood, we greeted each other cordially and I asked him what it was that they were doing there. They answered, quite reluctantly, that they were charged with sanitation; in other words, with the collection and transport to the cemetery of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just ask you a few questions about what you told us there. What -- what unit did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly which unit they belonged to at the time. I know that previously they were members of the anti-aircraft defence units. That's what they were members of back in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you notice if they had anyone who was particularly in command of them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't know who their commander was. I took it for granted that they had an order which they went about carrying out. I didn't stop to check that, nor was that my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what did you do, as a result of what they told you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: You know, sir, throughout the war, we feared pits. This is an old tradition from my native land. It was at all times important to us to bury dead soldiers and civilians according to all the standards in full respect of dignity. I -- that's why I went to see what this was all about. There was no order to that effect. I wanted to make sure that this was done properly, and we had to rely -- we had to be resourceful and creative in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just as a matter of information, for how long had you been involved in dealing with burials of dead bodies during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: As I joined the Operations Group Sinj at the end of 1994, and later on, when I joined Operations Group North, I was always present at the front line where, under the rules, the Croatian Army was duty-bound to carry out the proper removal of human bodies and carcasses. In other words, at the front line, I, as the chief of a medical corps, was the person responsible for it. Therefore, my arrival to Knin was nothing novel to me. It wasn't the first time. I had extensive experience, and, believe me when I tell you, that I was doing the job thoroughly and properly as of the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to the cemetery in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: As soon as I heard the information from this group of soldiers, I went to the cemetery right away. I didn't manage to find it at first, but I managed eventually, and it was at my second attempt that I succeeded. There was nobody at the cemetery, but at the end of the cemetery, I noticed an excavator. This convinced me that somebody was already engaged in sanitation and burying individuals. But I didn't find anybody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you with anyone when you visited the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No, I was on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you saw this -- this excavator, what did you see nearby?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: In its immediate surrounding, there was a hole that had been dug of approximate dimensions 4 by 4 metres. When I came to the edge of that hole, at the bottom of the hole I could see some eight, nine, or ten bodies laid down. I didn't exactly count them, I have to admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw the hole there with the bodies within, had there been any other signs within the cemetery of the digging of graves or any other place of interment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Not at the time. When I came there for the first time, there wasn't anything. I was simply there on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At that stage, on the 6th of August, whose responsibility was it for the burial and sanitation -- human sanitation in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Since Knin was not at the front line, all the burials, human sanitation were the task of the civilian protection of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I have some concerns about whether your question, line 11, 8, was well understood by the witness in view of his answer. I would just like to verify that. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I see what Your Honour mean, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, Mr. Kay asked you whether, when you came to the cemetery for the first time, whether you saw any other signs of the digging of graves. And from your answer, I take it that you understood the question to be whether you saw any persons digging graves. Is that how you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I understood that I was asked whether any other graves had been buried or whether any other preparations had been made for further interment. This was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I think it was included in the question as well, whether you saw any indicia of people having been buried there recently. The graves perhaps not prepared for being used, but perhaps already being used. Did you see anything which could be understood as indicia for recent opening of the ground and closing it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Current -- current burials.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Along the way that I walked on, so from the main entrance by the chapel, this is a rather wide passage, there were old graves on either side of this passage. But I did not walk anywhere else in the cemetery. I simply walked in the direction of the chapel and this is why, at that time, so in the morning hours of the 6th of August, to be more precise, it may have been about around 10.00, 10.30 in the morning on the 6th of August. It is rather difficult to recall exactly after so much time has lapsed, but bearing all in mind all my other duties at the time, I assume it may have been about 10.00, 10.30. So I did not walk around the cemetery but I walked directly in the direction of the excavator because this was what I was interested in. There were graves on either side of this passage, but I have to say, I did not pay too much attention. I was not interested in that. I was interested in the -- in the human sanitation itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to what you saw in the hole, the area that had been dug, was there anything that you could do at that stage to deal with the matter? You personally being there.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Well, quite obviously I couldn't do anything on my own. But it was quite clear that something needed to be done, and whoever did it before was unqualified for the job. And I have to say, when I recall these pictures today, I believe that they did it with the best of intentions. However, at that moment, I physically could not do anything on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What did you do next, having seen that -- that site? Where did you going?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I have to admit that, first of all, I didn't know what to do at all. The town was half empty. At that time we did not even have any internal communication. We could simply use couriers. So I went back to the hospital, and my intention was to try and get in touch with those who were involved with human sanitation. That is with civilian protection service, or whoever could do it from thereon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was that the civilian -- and was that the civilian protection run by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes. Short after I came back to the hospital, my driver brought me a message that members of the civilian protection came - he didn't know where from - and that they were getting ready for sanitation, as I was told at the time, and I quote: "To do it in our way." And this I understood to mean according to all the protocols, and my driver was aware of these protocols and rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And so what did you do next, in relation to this matter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: This information that the civilian protection took over the task the of sanitation, at that moment, was enough for me. And soon afterwards, we started with our next task, which we had to carry out, and this was to receive the medical team from Zadar which was supposed to come in and start managing the hospital. One part of that hospital was used by us as infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did you go to meet the incoming medical team from Zadar?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes. We waited for them there. Actually, we came to the Heliodrom with two vehicles with -- sorry, at the helipad with two vehicles in order to transport them from there to the hospital. The distance is rather long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did that happen? Did you meet the incoming medical team from Zadar and transport them to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact, did they arrive on a helicopter which also contained General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to your duties and responsibilities, did General Cermak have any role at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No. I recognised him at that time, because I simply knew him from TV or newspapers. I did not even know at the time what was the purpose of his visit, why he came there. I was explained that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Having taken the medical team to the Knin hospital, did you later revisit the Knin cemetery?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes. So, after we transferred the hospital, so to say, to the Zadar team, I was ordered to urgently inspect a situation along the road Knin-Bosansko Grahovo. I went there with my team, and in passing, we were on the road, but in front of the entrance to the cemetery, I could see a rather large group of people, and then I became personally convinced that these were members of the civilian protection that I heard earlier on were coming in, and they were organising their work, and we could see that from the road. In the afternoon hours, after I came back from my previous task, I personally stopped at the cemetery with my personal driver. The first thing I was interested in, as you can assume, is what happened with what I saw that morning; so, that hole with bodies laid in it and the excavator. At first, I was satisfied because I could immediately see that nearly half of the bodies were already taken out. Some four or five bodies, they were laid at a plateau in front and they were already put in body-bags. I introduced myself. They could see my insignia, the ranks, that I was an officer, so I asked them, I said that obviously I couldn't issue any orders. I was not a commander of theirs. But I asked them to complete their work there, and I said, Please, let us do the rest of this work according to all the rules and regulations of human sanitation. I went back a third time to see the situation as it was in the field, and then I already knew a person who said that he was either responsible or that he was coordinating that work. We jointly visited that group grave, mass grave, whatever you want to call it. I just wouldn't like to call it a pit. And that it -- the ground was levelled, and the bodies, at that time, were already buried in the left-hand side of the cemetery where there was still enough room, and that area, the left-hand side, looking from the entrance into the cemetery, was used for human sanitation purposes from there on in Knin. So the area where the hole was dug out previously was levelled. You could see that it was excavated sometime ago, or not so long ago. I was convinced then, if I may say so, I was so sure that the work was done properly that I even sent some beers to people who did that work in such difficult conditions, because the weather conditions were so difficult. It was very hot. And it is our custom that when you offer a drink to somebody, it means that you are expressing your satisfaction, and this is what I have done as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I could look at some of the detail there. Had -- did you discuss with the civilian protection team working there what you had found, what you had seen when you were there earlier in the day? Did you inform them about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did they tell you anything they had done about what you had seen, whether they'd taken any steps to deal with the problem that you had seen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I said already that when I came there for the second time, I could see already that approximately half of the bodies were taken out and were dealt with properly. Obviously I couldn't assume that they would leave the second half of the bodies in, because there was a large group of people there and a coordinator was there, so I can guarantee that I saw half of the bodies taken out, and I'm sure that they proceeded with the work in the same way, but it wasn't a pit in which the bodies were thrown but that was simply a way that somebody did a human sanitation task in an unqualified way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could you describe, then, the type of graves that were there that had been made by that civil protection team, how they dealt with it. Describe how they interred those bodies.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: The bodies were buried in a typical manner in which we usually do it when we bury bodies in the ground. So you have a grave dug out, you put in the body, and you have a small barrow on top, a small mound. When I came there for the third time, I tried to see what it was that they did, and I could see that there were graves, one next to another one. There was a cross on each of these graves, as we would normally put it above the head. The graves were typical graves dug in the same way in which it is customarily done in our country. It is done in this way, even today, if you bury somebody in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've described earlier the excavator. Do you know how the digging was done in the cemetery at that time? How this civil protection team dug?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: On that day, though I passed by the cemetery the next day -- but I'm not talking about that now. On that first day, people dug graves manually, and then I realised that the excavator I saw was broken down. It was out of order. The next day it still stood there in the same position, unmoved. I assumed that later on they brought new excavators and thereby they could work faster. But what I saw on the first day, it was done manually. This is very difficult work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you revisit the cemetery in Knin on any other occasions during the month of August?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Only once. I was asked by an acquaintance of mine who didn't know where the cemetery was and he wanted to visit a grave of a relative of his. So I took him there, but, on that occasion, I didn't even enter the cemetery. I smoked a -- and I smoked a cigarette in front of the entrance while he visited the grave that he wanted to visit. This was in the second half of August, and I didn't visit the cemetery on any other occasion because this was not a part of my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to now look at other -- another matter with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit P506, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, you'll see on that screen to the right again a document coming up that I want you to look at. You've referred to it in your statement. It's dated the 5th of August, 1995, from the Knin garrison, signed by General Cermak, and it contains your name within it. And I want you to look at this document with the Court. We can see that it says because of the situation that has arisen and the need for organised and expert human and animal hygienic and sanitary measures of the liberated region. And there's an order. And it says: "A field hygiene and sanitary measures staff is organised under the command of Garrison Town Knin composed as follows." And we see Brigadier Brkic, Chief of Staff; Dr. Gotovac, assistant chief for epidemiological affairs; Major Dr. Branko Sruk, assistant chief for human hygiene and sanitary measures. Now, you're named in this order. Were you ever part of a team that worked under the command of the Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: When you showed me this order, this was the first time that I ever saw it. So this was in the year 2009. I never was and I could not have been a member of a team, because my order, at the time, was to be chief of the medical team and commander of the operative team of the Operation Group North. On the 5th of August, I was still at the front line with the group of people that I presented to you earlier on. The last four members of this team, the last four names, are two nurses and two drivers, and they could not have been here, because that I would mean that I have been left without nurses and drivers, and I could not operate like that. The order that was still valid for me at the time, on the 5th of August and the 6th of August until probably 11th or the 12th of August, was as I previously stated. So it is rather clear that even if I wasn't a soldier, I couldn't have been at two places at once. My reports written on the 5th and on the 4th of August to my superiors were sent from the front line, and they clearly indicate that I could not have been here, no matter who issued this order. On the other hand, regardless of the fact that this order was signed by Mr. Cermak, even if I received it, at the time I could not have followed it, because I had an entirely different commander and entirely different orders. So although the military forces were only then being created, nonetheless nobody could go anywhere on one's own initiative. You had to follow the orders which you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll work up in reverse order, then, of the names here, as you identified those four who were part of your unit. Captain Boris Radovic, coordinator for animal hygiene and sanitary measures. Did you ever work during this time in a sanitation team with him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Up until that point, no. Subsequently, yes. However, at -- in this particular exercise contained in the -- referred to in the document, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if you could tell us, then, about Captain Radovic, what his role and job was and whom he worked for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Captain Radovic was, to put it simply, my counterpart. What I was in the medical corps, he was in the veterinary field. In other words, he was the chief of the veterinary service. It was only later, pursuant to General Gotovina's order of the 11th of August, that he was appointed the coordinator of the mixed team for sanitation, which was within the chain of command, something that came from the staff, and it was a fully valid unit based on the law. Mr. Radovic, who was a veterinarian, was appointed a coordinator. I suppose that were he now alive, he himself would confirm that he never saw the order that we have on our screens now, because he was unable to carry out two tasks at the same time and he had the same commander that I did. Therefore, there was nobody who could have ordered to us, save for our commanders. In other words, the commander of Operations Group North, and commander of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Captain Radovic, whom you said that you did later work with at that time, was that in connection with this order of the 11th of August you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. The operations and planning logistics from the Main Staff in Zagreb, bearing the signature of General Cervenko, an order arrived concerning the sanitisation -- sanitation of certain areas during and after Operation Storm. The order referred to all the Military Districts and addressed all those who were in the areas of responsibility under the direct command of the Main Staff. I suppose that the order reached Zadar, not Split, because the forward command post of the Split Military District was in Zadar at the time. An order was drafted there, which was signed by General Gotovina on the 11th of August, which contained all the elements of sanitation and everything else that was required in the area covered by the Split Military District, including Knin, as part and parcel of the AOR. At that time, Captain Radovic was appointed a coordinator. At that point, pursuant to the order which arrived from Zagreb, a mixed detachment was set up. It was quite clear to us that General Gotovina had signed the order whilst being fully aware of the vastness of the territory, which had a very small presence of individuals, most of whom had fled before or during Operation Storm. We were aware of the fact that we had to bring in completely new forces to deal with sanitation, be it the removal of human bodies, of carcasses, of any other debris, et cetera. It was an area where none of the facilities were operational. It was a true and proper order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just going up, then, to the next name on the list. Lieutenant Dr. Boris Samardzija. Do you know Lieutenant Samardzija?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes, I know him and I know everybody else very well. Boris Samardzija arrived only sometime on the 8th or 9th from Split. He took part in this exercise as a physician, and his primary role was in the reception centre that I told you about which we had set up on the hospital premises. Whether he was used for some duties other than those, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he used for any duties, in relation to sanitation of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And, again, is he an officer within the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes, he was an officer, member of the 306th Logistics Base in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to the next name, moving up. Snjezana Soldic, a vet. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes. She was a Miss, at the time, a Mrs. today. She was a veterinarian working in the health administration attached to the Ministry of Health. In other words, she was a civilian person who worked at the time for the Ministry of Defence. It was not customary for military personnel to issue civilians employed there any sort of orders. She was there for a couple of days, and it was more of a supervisory role that she had, and it was after the 10th or the 11th of August that she spent these two days in Knin. She stayed in home that was next to our infirmary housed in the hospital. She did not take any -- any active part in sanitation, and I don't really know what it is that she would be doing there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: She worked for the health administration within the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to your work, did you work with her at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've dealt with your position. Let's look at Dr. Gotovac, assistant chief for epidemiological affairs. Do you know Dr. Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Of course. In this initial phase of some ten days, Dr. Gotovac was not in Knin. He arrived only after the 10th or the 11th; roughly a week after Operation Storm. He is, indeed, a specialist in epidemiology, and he was also working for the health administration of the Ministry of Defence. However, his role at the time was as some sort of supervisor; in other words, he was supposed to oversee the sanitation process. I believe he even drew up a report. But he did not only come to Knin, he visited other Military Districts in the aftermath of Operation Storm. He could not have taken part in anything on the 5th of August, because he wasn't tasked to, and, again, he was an employee of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And lastly, Dr. Brkic, identified as Chief of Staff of this team. First of all, did you work with Dr. Brkic at all during this period in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: We came across each other on several occasions. I must admit that he tried, to put it that way, to coax these four people of mine, two drivers and two nurses, to join him. Now, of course, since we had completely different tasks that we were dealing, we were unable to cooperate. There was no need for it. And officially there was no cooperation. I received -- had I received an order from my superiors to establish any sort of cooperation, I would have. However, my superiors didn't even know that Dr. Brkic was forming any sort of staff and that he was engaging in sanitation, since we were all aware of the fact that it was the civilian protection that engaged in sanitation. It was a bit difficult at first because of the shortage of personnel, and it improved gradually. In other words, there was no need for any sort of staff. Ultimately, under the rules, under the law, this role should have been carried out by the civilian protection, because it didn't have to do, in this instance, with the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know exactly what Dr. Brkic was doing then in Knin? Perhaps if can I put the question in stages. You obviously know Dr. Brkic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know what he was doing in Knin at this time, what his task and responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: When I saw him first, I found it unusual, I must admit. I thought that it was merely a courtesy visit from members of the Ministry of Defence. I thought that he was there to give us a piece of advice. Otherwise, it was not customary for individuals from such a level to pay a visit to us, in order to directly engage in any sort of activity. Very soon, I realised that there was no order or rule based on which he would do anything there. Let me alert you to the fact that as part of preparations for Operation Storm, we knew directly from General Gotovina and other commanders what sort of action would be taken along which axes. And as I wrote instructions for logistics support, and therefore for sanitation as well, we knew that the sanitisation of an area that was outside of the direct combat zone, such as Knin, Drnis, Kistanje, et cetera, would be taken over by the civilian protection. Therefore, anything else would be in direct violation of the documents or the orders that we received from our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like you now to look at a report that he filed dated the 12th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit D30, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document referred to in your statement. Do you recollect there is this report and several other reports, one to Mr. Cervenko -- General Cervenko, one to Mr. Susak, one to General Gotovina, and you comment on them in your statement. I'm not going through each of them, but I'd like to you look at this one as being an example, and it is a report on sanitation and hygiene measures taken in the period. It refers to the 5th of August. And you've commented on -- on that order. And it refers to human sanitation measures. And he, in page 2 of the English, and in the main paragraph of the Croatian document, it refers to: "In Knin itself ... bodies of enemy soldiers were partially moved; namely, the rest could not be seen nor did they smell in view of the recent operation." And he refers to the church and finding an excavator with a large hole that had been dug with several bodies. And he refers to: "Aware that this was not the procedure to be followed, I issued an order to Mr. Ivan Jelic, engineer, to deal with the bodies in conformity with the Geneva Convention." That name there, Mr. Jelic, an engineer, is that familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The civil protection team that you came across on the 6th, would they be described as engineers or anything like -- like that? Do you know what the phrase here "engineer," or the word "engineer" refers to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Members of the civilian protection wore grey uniforms. I remember one of them. I think they were mobilised members of the Ministry of Defence. I don't think that they necessarily needed to be engineers. They were supposed to apply hygiene and sanitation measures in accordance with all the standards. The name doesn't ring any bells. I don't see why somebody should be an engineer or not. These were mobilised personnel. I realised a day later that they came from all over Croatia, including Zagreb. We were unable to man the team from among our ranks in Split and in the south, and I realised later on that MUP had taken upon itself to mobilise these people from across the country. This person, Jelic, if he was among then, I had never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We then go to the part of the report where the 6th of August, 1995, is referred to, and the fact that the president of the Republic arrived. And do you recollect that event, that President Tudjman arrived in Knin on that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes. I was not able to be personally present there. I told you that this was at the time when I was out in the field between the two visits that I paid to the hospital. I knew of the event. I don't see what it has to do with the report that was written, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the next paragraph, he refers to the morning of the 7th of August, 1995, arriving at the cemetery, finding the hole behind the church covered up. He received no answer as to who had done it. And it became clear to him that his presence was indispensable: "... due to the delicate nature of the work and other actions. The team formed, as can be seen from your order, took matters into its own hands and together with the civil protection staff produced results which conformed to all rules of hygiene and sanitation measures; that is, the bodies which were in a common room were separated and buried individually." Now we've looked at the team, and you've made your comments upon those individuals in the order dated the 5th of August. Just looking at that assertion here, that on the 7th of August, that team, which included you and some of your staff, took matters into its own hands and with civil protection staff produced results which conformed to all rules of hygiene and sanitation measures, and the bodies were separated and buried individually, on the 7th of August, 1995. As a relation -- in relation to that assertion in this report, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm just not sure that characterisation of when they were buried or separated and buried is accurate. If Mr. Kay could review that portion and perhaps readdress that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it says in the morning of the 7th of August, he arrived. He found the hole. He found that his presence was indispensable. The team formed, as can be seen from your order, and that's the order of the 5th of August, took matters into its own hands and together with civil protection staff produced resulted which conformed to all rules of hygiene and sanitation measures; that is, the bodies were separated and buried individually. It seems to me the assertion here that that is quite clearly on the 7th of August, his alleged team and civil protection dealt with the burial of these bodies individually as a team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mr. Carrier points at the line where it says: "The bodies which were in a common room were separated and buried individually." You left out the common room. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No. It's that Mr. Kay added that they were separated and buried individually on the 7th of August, 1995, taking the first part of the paragraph of and putting it on the last part of the paragraph and trying to make it seem that's what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that apparently is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- make anything seem anything, other than read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will redo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- phrase your question again perhaps by just literally reading, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you read this paragraph and you comment on it and tell us whether this event happened as described in the paragraph, Mr. Sruk.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Sir, may I comment on the entire report? Quite briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want you to comment on this paragraph and then I will give you an opportunity to comment on the entire report. But this paragraph which has this matter in it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You read it yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Kay. And then you asked the witness whether this event happened or not. Let's -- shouldn't we first ask whether he was present during such an event, and if the answer is yes, then, of course, he can comment on what happened. If the answer is no, then, of course, the witness may have other sources of knowledge on this event. But then at least we know what his source of knowledge is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you and the individuals identified in that order take part in the burial of those bodies that you described seeing on the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No. But the bodies were exhumed and then buried by the evening of the 6th. Mr. Brkic arrives on the 7th. He was not in Knin on the 6th. The first part is evidently a description based on the stories he heard. He arrives at the cemetery on the 7th, and it is true that he finds that the hole had been covered in, and he said that it's a delicate matter. But, you see, the problem lies in this. What would have happened, had the pit been covered in with the bodies inside? And this -- this is why I had always asked for my commanders to give me permission to give bodies a proper burial. So the bodies were disinterred and were then interred individually. They were given a proper burial. Already, on the evening of the 6th, the large hole had been filled in, and that's how he found it on the 7th. However, what preceded the prelude was different to what is explained in this report. And what's more suspicious is that the document doesn't even have a proper reference number, and this begs the question of what sort of report is this, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's all I ask on that matter, and you have dealt with the reports in your statement in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just trying to find the reference to the 11th of August order that the witness cited during his evidence, and I -- I noticed that I didn't mention to you which document he was referring to. It's Exhibit P496, which is part of his statement, and he dealt with it extemporaneously rather than looking at the document, and I wanted to link that up for Your Honour as to the particular document that was being cited by the witness. I hope that assists the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all I ask Mr. Sruk. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I first inquire with the parties as to how much time they would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, 20 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20 to 30 minutes, because we started on the basis of the assumption that Mr. Kay would take half a session where he took one session. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a session and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Session and a half. Which means that we have to be very efficient in order to finish at 1.30 p.m. Could the parties keep that in mind, that is, to get to the core of what they want to elicit as evidence from the witness without too many side roads. We'll first --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We revised our estimate to one session, as I recall, sent a notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I must have missed that. That's -- I'm just, at this moment, establishing what our real situation is, Mr. Kay, rather than to criticise. We'll have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sruk. I noted from your witness statement that you mentioned that you had been subordinated to OG North. Can you tell us, were you ever subordinated to Operative Groups Otric, Sajkovici, or Vrba.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D281 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, this is an order by General Gotovina dated the 9th of August, and it is his order for active defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 in the English. And if we could scroll down, please. Actually ... I'm sorry, it's page 5 in the English, at the bottom. If we could turn the page in English, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There you will see, Mr. Sruk, that on the 9th of August, General Gotovina ordered --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could scroll up in the Croatian, please. Sorry, if we could go -- page 4 in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if you look towards the middle of the page, in the Croatian, General Gotovina says: "Three operative groups shall be established for the defence, consisting of all forces and under the command of the Split Military District Command as follows ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And he renames and reforms the operative groups which as of 9 August become Operative Group Otric, Operative Group Sajkovici, and Operative Group Vrba. As of 9 August, Operative Group North ceased to exist. So after operative -- after 9th of August, can you tell us, who you would have been working for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: That's correct. On the 9th, or the 8th, or the 9th in the evening, the last briefing that I attended was in Sajkovici. At that time it still belonged to the Operative Group North. Thereafter, as I mentioned previously already, I came back to the 316th Logistics Base.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 306th Logistics Base.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my task was to continue to head the infirmary and medical station for members of the Croatian Army, which was set up in the building of the hospital that I previously talked about. So this is correct, what is stated here. Although I have to say that this is the first time that I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Dr. Sruk. I want to turn your attention now to your witness statement which is -- particularly at paragraph 6 -- sorry, paragraph 4 of your witness statement. And in that paragraph you mention that -- this is it at line 12 in the English: "I wrote two reports on my work to the commander of Operative Group North on 5 August 1995. Upon the delivery of the reports, I got a verbal order from the OG North staff to come to Knin immediately." I'd like to show you, Dr. Sruk, a few of the reports that you filed on the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have 65 ter 1D2997 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you will see on the screen that this is one report, on the 5th of August, that you filed with the commander of OG North. The report is titled: Report on killed, wounded and injured in Operation Summer 95 for 3 August 1995. Now, preliminarily, you do know that Operation Summer 1995 refers to the Grahovo operation prior to Operation Storm. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if you look through this document, if you look through the first page, it identifies wounded and injured of the 81st Croatian Army Guards Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page in both the English and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It also lists other injuries and then killed. It identifies five persons of the 81st who were killed, and then the sixth person is a member of the 4th Guards Brigade who was killed. So in terms of the report that you filed on the 5th, this -- this report, would have dealt with HV casualties in Operation Summer 95. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 1D2997 be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1740.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1740 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have on the screen, please, 65 ter 1D2998, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is, again, a report of the 5th of August to the commander of OG North, and the report is about killed, wounded and injured in Operation Kozjak 95 for 4 August 1995. That would be part of Operation Storm. And if we look through the first page, you identify wounded and injured of the 7th Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You then identify three members of the 7th Guards Brigade as having been killed in combat on the 4th of August. Mr. Sruk, would this have been -- looking at this report, is this, in fact, a report that you filed with Operative Group North on the 5th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1741.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1741 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, finally, Mr. Sruk, there was, in fact, a third report, and I will put that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 1D2999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is also a report of 5 August to the commander of OG North, report on killed, wounded and injured in Kozjak 95, for 5 August 1995. And if you look through that, you will see wounded and injured on the first page, members of the 7th Guards Brigade of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It also identifies two wounded or injured from the 4th Guards Brigade, several from -- two from the Special Police of the MUP of Herceg-Bosna and two members of the 4th Guards Brigade as having been killed. Is this a report, Doctor, that you in fact filed with Operative Group North on the 5th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, is it fair to say that the reports that you referenced in your witness statement, none of the reports that you filed on 5th of August related to -- to Serb soldiers or civilians being injured or killed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No. I did not come across them at the time. I did not have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 1D2999 be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1742.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1742 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you -- in your direct examination, you discussed General Cervenko's order on the 5th of August to form mixed sanitation teams. When was the first time that you actually saw General Cervenko's order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: It was after I received the order by General Gotovina dated the 11th of August. I heard the rumour that this order was in fact issued, that the order by General Gotovina was being prepared, and I asked for the original order to be delivered to me. Since this had to do with mixed teams and bearing in mind that I was a chief in the Operations Group North until the 9th, I asked for this, and I received it immediately after I received the order by General Gotovina on the 11th. This was the first time I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at General Gotovina's order from the 11th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have on the screen, please, Exhibit P496.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is the 11th of August order, referencing in the preamble, General Cervenko's orders of the 5th of August. And point 2 discusses the formation of operative groups for various towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to paragraph 4, which is the next page in this document, please. Numbered paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It identifies various tasks that need to be completed. You can see there, for example, point 4 is, the group must have -- I'm sorry. It describes who was going to comprise these groups. And paragraph 4.4 says a forensic technician and forensic operative. Paragraph 4.10 identifies persons for the clear-up of human bodies, five workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please. And we're going to have to flip back and forth a little bit, Mr. Registrar, I apologise for this. If we can go to, again, the next page, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You'll see that General Gotovina then says: "The personnel and equipment for items 4.5, 4.6, 4.7, 4.8, and 4.13 are to be provided ..." And then request we go down to 5f: For the Sibenik clear-up ... from the Sibenik squad of the 306th Logistics Base. Now, in answer to my first question, you had indicated that after the 9th of August you, in fact, had returned back to the 306th Logistics Base. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you keep in mind the numbers in the order as to what the -- what the Sibenik 306th Logistics Base was supposed to be doing, we need to look back at 4.5, 4.6, 4.7, 4.8 and 4.13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if we could flip back one page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So your logistics base was charged with providing an ambulance vehicle with a physician and medic, an ABKO squad with an M68 or M78 water truck; a combat security squad, engineers comprising of one combined trench digger and two drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then if we could turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And a personal vehicle for the commander of the clear-up of the operative group. And now if we scroll down to 6, paragraph 6, General Gotovina says: "Personnel and equipment for items 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.10, and 4.11 shall be provided by the Zadar-Knin county police administration, the Sibenik police administration, for item 5f, and the Split-Dalmatia police administrations for item 5g.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if we can go back now to the previous page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the MUP was charged with, under 4.2, having a Deputy Commander of the clear-up; 4.3 is an explosives expert; 4.4 was having a forensic technician and forensic operative; and 4.10 was the MUP was supposed to be providing the persons for the clear-up of human bodies of the workers. Now, this order, is that in fact how after the 11th of August the work tasks were divided, that essentially the HV was providing logistical support, and the MUP was providing the forensic technicians and the personnel to clear up human bodies?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Sruk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Carrier, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Sruk?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Carrier. Mr. Carrier is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, when you arrived Knin, were you aware that Dr. Brkic was already there, starting on the 5th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No. I saw him only on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So just to clarify, is it your position that he was not there; or you just didn't know whether or not, in fact, Dr. Brkic was already there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I arrived on the morning of the 6th. I'm not sure what had been happening on the 5th, and I saw him on the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to clarify your evidence today because at page 30, starting at about line 1 and on through half the page, with respect to the exhumation of bodies that took place in the cemetery, you said that Dr. Brkic arrived on the 7th, that he was not in Knin on the 6th. So is it that you just don't know if he was there on the 6th either, or the 5th or -- I mean, he could have been around, you just don't know? You're just assuming that here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: During the 6th, throughout the day, I was in touch with very many people belonging to the medical corps and sanitation teams, and it would have been very strange that I didn't come across him or that he didn't look us up in fact. So I cannot claim that he wasn't there, but I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Mr. Sruk, there's a lot more information in that answer that you just gave than was necessary. The answer is no, you didn't know whether he was there on the 5th or the 6th. You just don't know; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Zeljko Jonjic from the 306th Logistics Base?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Jonjic? Jonjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Jonjic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes, I do know a Jonjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And were you aware that he was temporarily assigned to the Knin garrison in August 1995 as assistant for logistics at General Cermak 's request?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Later on, seven or eight days later, I learned that he was assigned there along with some other people. But during the first four or five days, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: But during those first four or five days, did you see that person in and around Knin at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Earlier I saw him, but during the first four or five days that I spent in Knin, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, I just want to try to clarify something in your statement, and just let me know if I'm mischaracterising this at all, but is it fair to say that, in essence, your position is that, as far as you are aware, General Cermak was not officially involved in the sanitation operation conducted after Storm and that, as far as you know, he had no authority over those people that were conducting that sanitation operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: In the first four or five days, particularly in the first two days, he certainly had no authority, because he was never mentioned by anybody concerning this particular matter. Later on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, even -- even though you hadn't heard General Cermak mentioned in the first few days, it's just that you don't know exactly exam his role was, if he had any at all, with the sanitation operation being conducted. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I really do not know what was his role in respect to the civil protection. But everything that started about noon on the 6th was carried out by the civilian protection service of the Ministry of the Interior. What was his role in respect of them, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And with respect to Dr. Brkic, in your statement and during your testimony, you said that you're obviously aware that he was in Knin during August 1995. In your statement, you said you did not cooperate with him officially. And you said that during your testimony, that you weren't officially cooperating with him, and the same goes for, as far as I understood it, General Cermak, that you weren't ordered to do that, but you mentioned it as an official cooperation. Did you cooperate with either of these people unofficially or informally in any way, with respect to the sanitation operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: With General Cermak, no. I hardly saw him. Twice in Knin. Once when he came, and on another occasion I passed by him. When it comes to Dr. Brkic, I never cooperated him regarding the sanitation. Neither officially nor unofficially.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And just very briefly with respect to the order that you've looked at today with Mr. Kay and also during the time when you gave your statement, the order from General Cermak appointing you to the sanitation staff, you said today, I believe, that, you know, no one else or none of your superiors were aware of that order. Were you aware that when Dr. Brkic, in those reports that you also looked at during the time you gave your statement, had actually attached that order from General Cermak to those reports, and he sent them to Defence Minister Susak, Main Staff -- chief of the Main Staff, General Cervenko; the assistant minister for defence for logistics, Major-General Zagarac. He also sent it to the commander of the Split Military District, General Gotovina. He also sent that order to chief of civil protection, Mr. Cimiran. Were you ever aware or did you ever become aware of the fact that this order from General Cermak that appointed you had been circulating through all these people, some of which, if I'm not mistaken, are in fact superior to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: The order and the reports that you are mentioning, I saw them for the first time two months ago, when they were shown to me by Mr. Cermak's Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So even though all those names are mentioned in there, and you went through them today and picked out who they were and that you knew them, despite the fact that these were circulating around, you were never aware of it in any way. No one ever talked about it, no one filed a contemporaneous report, order or some kind of direction contesting that order. You are not aware of anything like that during the period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Sir, at the time, it was difficult to believe in rumours, and even if anybody told me something, I would not have believed it. The times were very serious. Unfortunately, or luckily, even the people belonging to my team, whom I mentioned previously, were not aware of this. Had they known about this, they would have told me so, and I probably would have acted upon it in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: During August 1995, did you ever attend any meetings that were held by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- could we seek a clarification of the previous answer, Mr. Carrier. You were asked whether you were not aware of anything like people talking about the order, or receiving a contemporaneous report. Then your answer was: "It was difficult to believe in rumours." And then later you said: "Even the people belonging to my team were not aware of this." Were there any rumours? Whether you believed them or not is another ... So you did not hear anyone talk about it, whether you believed it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, did you ever attend any meetings that were held by General Cermak during August 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Would you have any explanation if Mr. Jonjic placed you at meetings held by General Cermak during 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No. No, I certainly did not attend them. And for a long time, I was not aware of the location of the garrison command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sruk, I just want to clarify another part of your statement. And again correct me if I'm mischaracterising this. Is it fair that in essence your position with respect to Dr. Brkic is that effectively he was a self-promotor that went to Knin on his own accord, and he simply tried to adopted and report on the work of the people who were actually involved in sanitation operation, conducted during August 1995, to make himself look important?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: On the 13th or the 14th of August, 1995, Mr. Brkic was removed from his duty, at a time when he was still in Knin, which is yet another indication of the fact that he was there without the knowledge of his superiors, on his own initiative. How can one explain the date of the 5th of August, when General Cermak, or I, or any of those mentioned in the order were not there, nor did he know whether we were dead or alive? By that time, I had already spent four and a half years in the armed forces, and the fact is that my name was known in these circles. All these orders sent in -- in this chaotic way, without the respect for the chain of command, point me or lead me to conclude -- led me to conclude and still lead me to conclude that whatever he did was for his self-promotion by drawing upon the achievements of others and the jobs performed by others. When it comes to me, when I got there, I found that the job had been properly and thoroughly done by the civilian protection service in those four to five days before General Gotovina issued his order and some order was brought to the whole set-up. Now, the fact that there is mention of me in these reports sent to the Main Staff and Generals, I believe is completely misplaced, because I was not there. When we first had the occasion to get acquainted with Mr. Brkic, it all became quite clear to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, you say that he was removed from his duty on 13th or 14th of August, 1995. I'm not aware of that. Can you explain that a bit more? Who removed him? How do you know about that? What is your actual knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: The documents shown to me confirm this, although I don't have an order to that effect, or as the ministry would normally issue decisions, I can only see his signature in a report where he reports to the chief of the Main Staff, General Cervenko, on all these tasks that had been referred in the various reports referenced by Mr. Kay here. This goes to prove that he was no longer the chief of the health administration of the Ministry of Defence, but, rather, that he was transferred to the staff. Let me tell you that the hierarchy --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Brkic [sic], I'm going to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: -- in the ministry, although it was not a military hierarchy --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you off, Mr. -- sorry, Mr. Sruk, I have to cut you off because it is not really answering the question. It is a very specific question. I'd like to know without assuming anything, because now you're coming up with an explanation based on assumptions, what specifically do you know about him being removed from his post on the 13th or 14th of August? And do you actually know that, or are you just assuming it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No, I know this for a fact. I don't know the exact date. Now, what I was trying to explain to you just now is that in the documents that exist - I have them in my bag here, and they were shown to me by Mr. Cermak's Defence a couple of months ago - you can see that he no longer signed with the title of the chief of health administration of the Ministry of Defence but as a chief in the staff. I have a document indicating this. I don't know it off the cuff, but if you show it to me, I can indicate that section to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, what you're actually doing is drawing conclusions from a difference in the way that documents were signed by Mr. Brkic. Do you have any other knowledge, that is, direct knowledge, that could be -- well, could perhaps be explained in many ways. But do you have any other specific knowledge of Mr. Brkic being removed from his job?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
