utterances.text: Your Honour, there is reference in the Brkic reports to: "I hope I have justified my presence. Dr. Zdilar has helped me a great deal. For instance" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I give you the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's in these multiplied reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay. There are two different matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first is what this witness knows and from what sources. And the second is, I mean, I can state something where it's unclear where my knowledge comes from, even whether I have proper knowledge, which does not necessarily mean that what I'm say something not correct or true. Nevertheless, I would appreciate if you give me the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it's relevant to the question if the witness is being tested on his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- if you give me the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: D1060, page 2 in the English. If you go to P543, last page in the English. And it's a phrase that's repeated in these reports that he sent around. That's all I say. I don't know whether the witness is being challenged or whether the fact is being challenge. But it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That's -- that is still -- as a matter of fact, I wasn't challenging any fact. I was just -- where Mr. Carrier asked the witness what the source of his knowledge was, I then verified whether this was the exclusive source or whether he had any other source of knowledge. That's what we were doing, and now you're pointing us to the substance of what the witness said, and I -- I'm glad to -- to verify that. But that's a different matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, in relation to your characterisation of Dr. Brkic, you also state that General Cermak did not have enough knowledge to know what it was that Dr. Brkic was doing, in effect. Can you explain your factual basis for knowing what it was that General Cermak actually knew about what General Brkic was doing or anything else to do with the sanitation operation happening in Knin during August 1997 -- or 1995.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I said that General Cermak evidently didn't have all the information, because he signed an order with me as the Deputy Chief for sanitation; whereas, I had different commanders. My chain of command was a different one, which led me to conclude that he was not privy to the facts or that the facts were not presented to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So just to be clear, is it fair to say that you don't know exactly what General Cermak knew about the sanitation operation or exactly what his relationship was with Dr. Brkic during August 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I don't know the extent of his knowledge or the nature of his relationship with Dr. Brkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, I just want to turn now to the -- that hole you saw in the Knin cemetery again. And I think we've sorted it out. You weren't really sure when Dr. Brkic was in Knin in early August 1995, yet in your statement and today, you're describing a situation where you're saying that you're sure that those bodies that you saw earlier in the day on the 6th of August had been buried properly, and that basically you're saying that Dr. Brkic's account of this instance is not true, that you know basically that these bodies were properly buried on the evening of the 6th of August. And so there is no way that all these reports where Dr. Brkic is reporting on an improper burial, those are all incorrect. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I said and described what I saw. Now, what Dr. Brkic saw and when, I don't know. The dead bodies were disinterred from the hole and buried in accordance with the standards. What I don't know is whether they were registered and identified. I know that the bodies were individually buried and that the hole was filled in. Suspicions are merely suspicions. I'm describing what I saw with my own two eyes. I'm not telling you the stories I heard from others. I was lucky enough to see the end result, and I am still proud of the fact that we were able -- or, rather, other people were able to do it properly and that I was able to witness it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it there would be absolutely no reason for the Ministry of Interior to dig up those bodies again on the 11th of August and rebury them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: The question is this: Given your testimony and your statement, that you went to -- well, in your statement you went to the Knin cemetery twice. During your testimony you went three times to basically witness this proper burial of bodies, which you initially saw a hole that wasn't proper, and you went back. You wanted to make sure it was going to be done properly, and you're testifying that it was done properly. My question is: If that is what happened, then you can think of no reason why Dr. Brkic would be ordering that the hole that he was referring to be dug up and the bodies be buried properly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I have never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have document number 65 ter 7162 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, what's going to come up on the screen is a report from the chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration, Mr. Cetina, dated 12 August 1995. And if you look at this report, Mr. Cetina indicates that on orders from Dr. Brkic, an exhumation took place on the 11th of August, 1995, in the Knin cemetery, in respect of bodies that were buried before the 7th of August, 1995, contrary to the regulations of international law. Mr. Cetina describes transferring bodies and burying them in appropriate places and changing certain identification numbers. So my question for you, Mr. Sruk, is: How do you reconcile your observations of the 6th of August and your testimony that these were properly buried with Mr. Cetina's report about bodies being exhumed and transferred for burial in appropriate place on the 11th, on orders of Dr. Brkic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm seeing this. I don't know if it refers to the same site. I don't know if something was done subsequently. I can stand by what I said and saw, which was that the matter was dealt with properly. What this was about, I really don't know. I have never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So am I to understand your evidence is now that you're not sure if the hole you saw is now the same one that you had referred to earlier as the one that Dr. Brkic was talking about. It could be a different one, a different site. I think we can agree it's the Knin cemetery, though; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: The pit I was referring to and have been discussing all along has been clearly identified by me. It was right next to the gate and to the chapel. This is the detail I was discussing. Whether there were others, that's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And given the document, can you offer any explanation as to how it is that Dr. Brkic is issuing orders to people involved in the sanitation process, specifically members of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I didn't want to comment on it. I find it strange. It wasn't either customary or envisaged by any rules. The MUP is a civilian organisation; the armed forces and the Ministry of Defence have a separate chain of command. How this came about is something I cannot comment on. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask that that document be marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2652.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, would you have any explanation as to why General Cermak would say to Prosecution investigators that Dr. Brkic was in charge of the Knin cemetery with respect to burial of bodies during the beginning of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sruk, just to be fair to you, is it just that you don't know really anything about who was in -- or specifically in command and control, issuing orders, instructions, that type of thing, to the civil protection bodies involved in sanitation operation after Storm?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. I don't know about the first one or two days. Later on, it was Mr. Cicak. And to the best of my knowledge, he was in command of or in charge of or coordinating his -- I cannot call them units. His department -- or how should I call it? I don't know what the title was, the civilian department, and he ran the department. I know that he was coordinating these activities. I wouldn't say that he was in command. I don't know what the official terminology of the time was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And -- sorry, is that Mr. Cicak or Mr. Cicko?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I think his name is Cicak. Cicak. Cicek.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So if I suggest to that you Damir Cicko was actually the representative of the Ministry of the Interior coordinator for the sanitation of Knin, you don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It has to do with him. But, you see, it's been 15 years. Whether it was Cicko or Cicek, it's the same as with Jonjic or Janic. We agreed that it was one and the same person we had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And do you know a person named Damir Cimiran. This is the assistant -- the chief of the civil protection. And he was, according to Assistant Minister Zidovec, the main civil protection official on the ground after Operation Storm, and he was tasked with supervising and coordinating the work of civil protection units on the ground. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No. I wasn't a member of any team charged with coordinating. What happened on the evening of the 6th was the extent of my intervention into the sanitation process in Knin, excluding the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So I take it, then, you would have no information about Mr. Cimiran reporting to the Assistant Minister who's the head of civil protection, Minister Zidovec, where he actually references to Dr. Brkic in reports and interactions between Dr. Brkic and civil protection, and even cites some disagreements between or disagreement at least between Mr. Cicko and Dr. Brkic with regard to how to bury bodies. You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Not from personal knowledge. I was told that there were confrontations, conflicts and misunderstanding. I can't confirm them. I only heard about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And you're talking about conflicts between individuals and groups involved in the sanitation process, and those people having conflicts with Dr. Brkic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I'm referring specifically to the conflict between Mr. Cicko and Dr. Brkic. I'm not referring to groups. I'm not aware of there being more than one group, and that was the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sruk, in -- were you aware that soon after this report I just referred to, from Chief Cimiran about the conflict between Mr. Cicko and Dr. Brkic, that General Cermak specifically requested that Mr. Cicko be transferred from civil defence or civil protection on to his staff for the sanitation in the Knin garrison? Do you have any information or do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't know anything about it. I saw a piece of information two months ago when I was presented some documents. I wasn't aware of it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we see the document that has been cited by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, can you assist Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to D1058.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sruk, you mention one of the things when you reviewed that request was that you said that General Cermak didn't have the authority to issue orders to two people, specifically Mr. Radovic or Ms. Soldic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have document number 65 ter 55 -- sorry, if we could have Exhibit D610 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sruk, what you're going to see on the screen in front of you is actually an order issued by General Cermak to both of those people to whom you said he doesn't have the authority to do that. And that's in relation to sanitation of the terrain in Knin, and it's copying Dr. Brkic at the bottom. Does that change your mind at all about General Cermak's authority to issue orders to those people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I'm not changing my mind. He could not issue such orders. Now, there is no signature or initials, so I can only assume that he ordered this to Mr. Radovic and Madam Soldic in the same way in which he issued an order to me. But he couldn't do it because the command line was totally different. So obviously this was ... this was supplanted to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: But is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, can I ask you, you say there is no signature. Could you explain that answer, in view of what I see on the screen? Apart from whose signature it is, but I see something which appears to me to be a signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please let me explain. You probably did not understand what I was saying. On the left-hand side, it was customary for those of who wrote proposals of orders as associates of our commanders on the left-hand side to put our initials. First of all, you had initials of person that authored the proposal/the person who actually wrote/typed the proposal. For example, if I was drafting this particular document, on the left-hand side just above this where it says, To, to whom it should be delivered, it would be written BS/BS. Everybody knew that this meant that I authored the document. The person who signed the document and the person who would receive the document knew it. So, until the commander signed it, it was just a proposal. And this would mean that I authored and that I actually typed it. If I didn't type it in person, then the initials of another person would be next to mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, I have no problem in hearing your testimony about what you would expect on a -- on an order, as far as who would have drafted that and whether you would find initials. You said there's no signature. The only question I asked you is what I look at this document, I see a signature. So apart from -- I didn't ask you any question about the absence of initials. I just asked you about what you said about the signature. Anything to add, in relation to the signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there may have been a misunderstanding. I said that there were no initials. I did not refer to the signature that you can see on the screen. So it was a misunderstanding. When I was saying I was actually indicating that there should have been initials, and on top of that, the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Did you say -- because I'm a bit confused about your last answer. You said: "I said that there were no initials. I did not refer to the signature that can you see on the screen." So you didn't use the word "signature" apart from the word "initial"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that we would have to ask our transcribers or our interpreters why they make a mistake, or is it possible that you use the word "signature." We can consult the original words you used. Are you certain that you did not use the word "signature" in your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did use it, but I did not refer to this signature, to another signature that I explained later on, and that was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you be very careful in even suggesting that our interpreters and our transcribers are not properly doing their job. I would have expected your answer to be, I used the word "signature" but in a different context, and then you could have explained that. Whereas you suggested that you did not use that word. But now I hear that you did use that word, so that, therefore, our transcribers and interpreters are doing their job properly. Is the message clear, Mr. Sruk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Just where we left off, Mr. Sruk, you said that, as far as you know, General Cermak didn't have the authority to issue these orders. But you have already told us that you don't really know what General Cermak's authority was, what his relationship was to specific people, for instance, Dr. Brkic, what his relationship was with the civil protection. So can you explain what your actual factual basis is for -- for testifying that General Cermak couldn't issue these types of orders to these people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: As far as I knew by then, the commanders of garrisons were not in the same command line with unit commanders. If I have a commander, and Mr. Radovic has it, and if they have a superior assistant for logistics at the ministry, Madam Soldic, it follows for me, and particularly now when I saw all of this, that General Cermak, as a commander of the garrison, could not issue orders to these people without having consulted other instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sruk, I thought we covered this off, but let's go through it quickly. Do you -- or did you, during August 1995, ever learn the details of who it was that actually had appointed General Cermak to his position in Knin?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that. It -- I was not interested in that either, because my tasks were entirely different. I was not a politician but a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. Stop. I'm cutting you off, sir. I'm cutting you off because the question wasn't about what you were interested in; it's about what you know. So it fair to say that you did not know the precise parameters of the authority or the tasks that had been assigned to General Cermak in Knin in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So given that answer, how can you accurately or honestly give any answers about what kinds of orders or to whom General Cermak could issue orders during August 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: It is difficult to describe briefly the rules of the game, so to say, of what the Croatian Army was doing. If I had an order which --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Please allow me to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, it is fair to the witness that can he briefly explain what he means. Could you briefly explain what is the basis on which you can give your opinion or assessment of the competence of Mr. Cermak issuing orders, like the ones we've looked at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As I started to say, until then, I had a valid order, and my commander was the commander of the Operations Group North, and I had clear instructions as to what to do. All of a sudden, without my knowledge, there comes somebody else who issues an order of an entirely different nature, of an entirely different type, and a different field of activity. From this comes my statement when I said that even if I knew about this order on the 6th of August, 1995, I could not have implemented it, because my old orders were still valid. Such were the rules of the game.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it's not an answer to what Mr. Carrier asked you, I understand your position to be that, since you had no reason to believe that Mr. Cermak would have the authority to issue orders which were contradicting the orders you earlier received, that -- if would you have been aware of this order, you may not have implemented it. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's move on, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, with respect to the sanitation operation happening in and around Knin during August 1995 and following, is it not the case that the Knin garrison was responsible for organising, among other things, the logistics for that operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Until August the 11th, when the order was issued by General Gotovina, then it became clear who is supposed to provide logistical support to whom and for what. Until then, all that I knew was that civilian protection of the Ministry of the Interior was in charge and was carrying out sanitation tasks. Who supported them, I really don't know. Where they got their shovels, I don't know. I know they had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sruk, I'm going to suggest to you that, in fact, the Knin garrison was involved in not only coordinating logistics but also issuing instructions and other types of information regarding the sanitation operation occurring in and around Knin during August and September 1995.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Thank you for this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You don't dispute that; you just don't know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I'm not sure where the garrison, during this first four or five days, could be able to find logistic support and provide logistic support to anybody given the situation in Knin at the time. So I'm talking about the first four or five days. I'm talking about what I know but I'm not certain. So it is my assumption, based on what I know and what I saw. I'm not sure where could I find any support or equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sruk, they found it, I think, in your home base, the Sibenik Logistics Base. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, following General Gotovina's order of August the 11th. But for the first three or four days, I doubt it. I know that the civilian protection brought their own uniforms, equipment, everything they needed, including trucks. And everything else they brought themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So you don't dispute that the Knin garrison was certainly involved in assisting with the sanitation process --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has answered this question in many different forms. It's not a question to say -- the way it is put, "So you don't dispute that," that's not the way of questioning him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I think that the position of the witness in relation to the matter you raise in your last question is clear. If there is any specific point you would like to further address, you can do so. But we're now, again, back in the rather general -- in a rather general assessment of the situation, which has proven to -- to create more confusion than clarity. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was about to get into some specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, were you aware of any kind of communication happening between civil defence or civil protection units making certain complaints and then the Knin garrison, in turn, acting on that and rectifying those complaints. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, would it help to put a time-frame to your question, that is, up to the 11th of August, because that might play a role.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: During any time in August or September 1995. And I can give a couple of examples, one of which Dr. Brkic requesting 350 crosses for the burial of -- referred to as Chetniks. Putting together eight boilers so that the civil protection staff can shower in Knin, which seems to be in response to a complaint made by the chief of civilian protection, Mr. Cimiran. I'm just wondering whether you're aware of anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it possible to add, for the Chamber's information, dates to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: It's, for reference purposes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: It's in D1015, which is the 29 September 1995 report on logistics from Mr. Jonjic. The dates are not specific. It just gives a general list of things they were doing, so it is not specified by date, but, rather, a range of dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, do you think any about the 350 crosses or the -- making shower facilities or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was a major charged with orders issued by my superiors for very specific tasks. I have no idea about shower facilities or crosses that were requested by anybody. I mentioned previously I saw some ten crosses in the cemetery. They were placed appropriately where the graves were. There was no way I could have known about this because I still claim that I never belonged to any of the logistic teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know, unless there are any further questions on your knowledge, just tell us that you don't know, and then whether you should have known is a totally different matter. There's no need to explain why you do not know what you say you do not know. Please proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, turning to Dr. Gotovac. You remember that person you discussed today. You mentioned that he is from the Ministry of Defence Health Administration. Now, you're also aware that Dr. Brkic was actually the chief of that health administration, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And what you describe in relation to Dr. Gotovac is that there was an official role being fulfilled by Dr. Gotovac, in terms of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I just want to find the reference. It's just at the end of page 23 of today's testimony, onto page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: That that person was there to oversee the sanitation process during August 1995. Now, my question is: If this person, Dr. Gotovac, who was subordinated to Dr. Brkic, is doing that, I'm going to suggest to you that in fact that's also what Dr. Brkic was there doing, was to oversee the sanitation process and make suggestions for how to improve it, et cetera, as it went along.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: The part in which I mentioned Dr. Gotovac, I said that he was in charge of monitoring. Let me explain. He visited the entire field and he reported on what he saw. So what was being done, in which way, and what should have been done. He did not participate directly in the sanitation activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And what I'm suggesting is that his job and Dr. Brkic's job was to actually oversee that process. Is that fair? And if -- to refresh your memory, we could look at a document you looked at in your statement, which is D1059, which is a report signed by both Dr. Brkic and Dr. Gotovac, dated the 12th of August, 1995, sent to General Cermak. And if it helps you out at all, there is also another document that's in evidence which is a report dated the 20th of August, 1995, which is over a week after you say Dr. Brkic was removed, which is a report sent to Dr. Brkic from Dr. Gotovac, and that's P2572, which indicates that their activity after Operation Storm was a regular duty of the health administration; namely, to supervise the professional work related to human sanitation. It also mentions that they acted pursuant to an order of the chief of the Main Staff. Dr. Gotovac, as you state, recounts a reconnaissance of the human sanitation operation. It also mentions that where discrepancies were detected from the established practice, verbal instructions were issued to both the police and the civil protection members, in order to eliminate such failures, and those people in turn gave assurances that such failures would be eliminated. And this is also consistent with how Dr. Brkic starts off all of his reports to all those high-placed Croatian authorities saying, That this is the regular task of his administration. So my question to you: Isn't it, on the basis of these documents, do you have any information about whether or not Dr. Brkic's role was to oversee the sanitation process, just like you say Dr. Gotovac was doing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Could I kindly see the document that you have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes. You can see it. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could you call up Exhibit P2572 onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Sruk, just so -- for your reference, the other document I had referred to -- I believe you said you have documents with you, but that's the one that's countersigned by both Dr. Brkic and Dr. Gotovac, and that's dated the 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Could I kindly see the end of this document? Yes, could I see the very end of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And it may assist, the -- I believe the actual document has an attachment. But there's three pages, I think, and then there's a signature at the end. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go through the document, starting on the third page, to see whether we ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I see the beginning of this document that I just have on the screen now? Yes, here you have the results of the work of the control inspection, or supervision. This is what is clearly stated here. I apologise. Could I see if this document was listed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would please look at the documents as requested but listed -- it's unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would kindly ask the witness to repeat his request. But this is what was stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please repeat what you said last. You said: "I apologise. Could I see if this document was ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to see the entire document, because I can only see the first page here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest the following, Mr. Carrier. Let's have a break. Let's make hard copies of the documents you want to show to the witness. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Actually he asked to see it. I did the courtesy of showing it to him, but it was just a question about, if that's what's in the document, then how does he explain Dr. Brkic's role. So, that's the only information I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. But apparently the witness would prefer to answer the questions once he has seen the document in its entirety, and that's -- if it's a three-page document, then I think it should not create a major problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- on behalf of my client, and I'm certain the others as well, they haven't been able to follow the documents because they're being summarised quickly. And then now they would also like to see the documents so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's then take our time and perhaps make one or two copies as well for the accused of the original so that we know what we are talking about. I would rather not hear any evidence where the witness is hesitant to say anything unless he has seen this three-page document in its entirety. If could you take care of that, Mr. Carrier. Then you know of our time constraints. Could you tell us how much time you would still need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: As you can tell, I'm trying to go quickly. But I should be done in 20 minutes, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20, 25 minutes. Could I get an estimate on time needed for re-examination, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's none at the moment, other than a very short matter within five minutes. It's not substantial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing arises until this moment. We will have a break. Mr. Carrier, you are invited to provide hard copies. And we will resume at five minutes to 1.00, sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And in the interests of time, I would like to, at the end of this session, bar table document 65 ter 7452, which is a 12th of August, 1995, report from Brkic to Cimiran. It's similar to all the other ones, but if my friends have the chance to look at it, perhaps we can address it at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I just ask you, I did write down for myself that P2652, which is the -- I think, Brkic says that it corrects the report on what was done on the 11th. Is the original report available as well, apart from the correction being there, whether that gives any additional information?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm not aware of one, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you noticed that it says it is the correction on the report and -- of the 11th and a report on what was done on the 12th. That's in the title at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I believe we can find them. It may just be in relation to body lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be. But it could describe what happened. Whereas here we may find, for example, further details on re-numbering the -- the bodies identified. If could you find that, it might assist. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, we left off -- you had a chance to look at the document; right? Now my question is very simply, given this report to Dr. Brkic from Dr. Gotovac, do you actually know whether or not Dr. Brkic was also involved in supervisory reconnaissance of a human sanitation operation conducted after Storm by members of civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: It does not follow from this document. However, I know that Dr. Gotovac visited various places and oversaw the process, and at the end of that overseeing procedure, he drafted a report. He was on his own at the time. And I'm referring to the professional overseeing of the work of the members of the ministry. And this was standard procedure. And I'm glad that you showed me the document. This confirms that the agreement on the competence of the civilian protection, complete with all standards of work, was honoured, because Dr. Gotovac states that there was an agreement for the civilian protection --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, I'm going to cut you off. Mr. Sruk, I apologise. I'm under time limitations and my question was very simple. It was about whether or not you actually know whether or not Dr. Brkic, who's being reported to by Dr. Gotovac in this report, was also involved in that supervisory reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: The -- of the work that was carried out in Knin, he was not. For the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And on what exactly do you base that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I was in Knin at the time when the supervision took place. I spoke to Dr. Gotovac who phoned me. So I know, I am aware of the time when he was involved in this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: That's just Dr. Gotovac, though, right? You're talking about you're aware of when Dr. Gotovac was involved.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Yes. What follows from the document, what he did. This particular supervision exercise. It was earlier. The report is of the 28th, and Dr. Gotovac was in Knin on his own, and he told me about the problems that existed in Knin and around Knin and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have D598 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, what's coming up on the screen is General Cervenko's order of the 5th of August, 1995, calling for sanitation by mixed sanitation detachments of the territory where Storm was conducted. Now, you have had a chance to look at this document already. But my question is, Mr. Sruk, can you point specifically - and before do you that, I'm going suggest that you won't find them - to the words "area of combat activities," or "front line," or "battlefield," where those are used in this order to indicate that the activities of the mixed sanitation detachments that are being set up under this order are limited to operating in those types of areas?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we get a cite, and it may very well be true, but where the witness said that the mixed sanitation detachments only operated on the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Area of combat activities I think you can find in paragraph 5, line 29, page 3 of the English. It says "during combat activities." Paragraph 6, line 6, page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, but that's different than what -- the way the question is posed. The Prosecutor is suggesting that the witness said that mixed combat groups were only operating at -- in the combat, and that's different than what is said in paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I was actually not finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Carrier is now aware that Mr. Misetic thinks that the -- focussing on those portions of the testimony in which reference is made to limited areas that that's important to include that in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And for the record, the question was finished and he was asked to point in this to order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry. I meant that I wasn't finished citing the other instances. But if you are not worried about that, I'll just ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, is it not your position that the mixed sanitation detachments operated in -- on the battlefield, or areas of combat activities, or the front line, and that's where they were supposed to be operating?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I have never stated that, nor could I have. Pursuant to this order and General Gotovina's order which had to do with his AOR of the Military Districts, the mixed detachments were set up to be used everywhere except for the combat zones, because the sanitation in the combat areas was carried out by the Croatian Army. And that's quite clear. The mixed detachments were set up in addition to the military units, and they were civilian, in order to cope with the vast territory. And I -- I wouldn't dream of stating what you've just -- the word that you have just put into my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. So they operated everywhere; that's fine.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No, no. I repeat, no, they did not. It was the Croatian Army that did the job in the battlefield, according to the orders. The mixed detachments established pursuant to this order of the 5th of August by the chief of the Main Staff were active throughout the territory, save for the combat zones. And that's quite clear. There is a clear distinction. Civilians have no place being at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Sruk, when you gave your statement, you reviewed a number of documents. And then you confirmed that the mixed sanitation teams sanitised the terrain in the Split Military District during August 1995. And you said that the chain of command and reporting was fully respected in accordance with General Cervenko's order - the one we're looking at here - and also General Gotovina's order dated the 11th of August, 1995, which is P4 -- sorry, P496.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if we could actually just have P496 on the screen quickly. And if you could turn to page 2 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, you were shown this document during the

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: identified who was responsible -- responsible for providing different aspects of these mixed sanitation groups. In terms of 4.1, the commander, is it fair to say that the commander of these groups is an HV member?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: According to what is stated here, yes. And he was, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Sruk, with respect to the report sent by Dr. Brkic, which you reviewed, in your statement you said that Dr. Brkic did everything aforesaid in contrast to the order of the Chief of the Main Staff, General Cervenko, of August 5, 1995, in which the tasks for carrying out sanitation and coordination of HV with the police administration civil protection and health crisis staff of the counties in the liberated areas were clearly stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we could go back to Exhibit D598 which, just for reference --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, this is General Cervenko's order again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 4 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Looking at item number 7, Mr. Sruk, if you have a chance to look that over, is it fair to say that item number 7 of General Cervenko's order very generally sets out some of the individuals and bodies that are responsible for coordination and supervision of the participants in the sanitation campaign conducted in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question. If you have not understood it, we will invite Mr. Carrier to repeat it. Mr. Carrier characterised what he thinks is found in paragraph 7, and he is seeking whether you agree or disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, I didn't understand just now what it was about. This is the normal channel of communication and reporting, where the chief of the Main Staff charges the operational logistics, that's to say, the chiefs of the medical corps, Dr. Marijan Zlatar -- that's to say, the chief of the medical corps, Dr. Marijan Zlatar, and the chief of the veterinarian profession, Perajica, to report to him on the sanitation carried out throughout the territory affected by Operation Storm. That's quite clear and quite proper. And only goes to show that all the others were outside of this order which came into force on the 5th of August. Do I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood the question. What Mr. Carrier would like to know is whether you agree or do not agree with, as he put it to you, that paragraph 7 of General Cervenko's order very generally sets out some of the individuals and bodies that are responsible for coordination and supervision of the participants in the sanitation campaign conducted in August 1995. Is that a fair statement, that that's to be found in paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Judge, this is an order by the then-chief of the Main Staff. This is a usual procedure of issuing commands, where he charges the -- his immediate subordinates with coordinating and ensuring the implementation of the order. I cannot comment on the order of the chief of the Main Staff, but I can only tell you that it is fully within the spirit of the orders issued at the time, where who is responsible for what is quite clearly defined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sruk, just to direct your attention more specifically to the last paragraph under item number 7, which states that: "All unclear issues shall be resolved in coordination with the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia Health Administration." Now, Mr. Sruk, given that Dr. Brkic was the head or the chief of the Health Administration, I'm going to suggest to you that you he was responsible under this order to coordinate the resolution of all unclear issues, in respect of the sanitation campaign, which means that any of his orders, input, direction, et cetera, related to accomplishing that in a sanitation campaign would have to be given due weight and attention, which -- perhaps you could comment on. Is that not fair? Is your characterisation of Dr. Brkic's role inconsistent with that, or you just don't know what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I disagree with your assertion. It is quite clear -- I'm trying to account for the system that was in place at the time. All the things that were unclear and that stemmed from General Cervenko's order were to be clarified with the competent authorities, and, at the time, it was the ministry. This was standard procedure. But it only had to do with those elements that were unclear. On the 5th of August, there were no such things that were unclear yet. When they emerged, they were being dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, let me ask you, what specifically are you basing your testimony on, that -- that -- on the 5th there was nothing really that was unclear? What information were you getting, who was reporting to you, how would you actually know that? And how would you know whether or not the Health Administration would be involved in any of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Quite simply on the 5th of August, none of the members of the medical corps were present in Knin. The only person who arrived was my chief of -- within the Military District who flew in by helicopter and then went away again. Nobody came after him, until the early morning hours, when I, together with my teams -- well, it wasn't the -- at the crack of dawn; it was at 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning - that I arrived. And it is quite certain that no one was aware of any problems on the 5th. What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is set out here is the normal course that the issuing of an order would entail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I understand your answer to be that you were not aware of any unclear issues on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please -- could you please move on, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, on the basis of your review of Dr. Brkic's reports during your statement, you concluded that Dr. Brkic was not acquainted with the work of the mixed teams for sanitation on the liberated areas, said he wasn't familiar with the fact that these teams reported on their work to the OPL at the Main Staff of the Croatian Army in Zagreb on a daily basis. Now, Mr. Sruk, other than the reports that you looked at from Dr. Brkic, that you looked at for the first time in September 2009, what is your factual basis for saying that Dr. Brkic was unacquainted with the work of the sanitation teams or where it was that they reported to? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Having received General Gotovina's order, and once the mixed teams were set up -- or, rather, let me correct myself, not teams but detachments. The commander of the detachments reported along his chain of command up to the chief of the medical profession of the Split Military District. They, in turn, reported to the operations and planning of the logistics within the Main Staff in Zagreb, and it was the individuals listed in item 7 who received the information. And that was the proper implementation of the order issued by the chief of the Main Staff, by the commander of the Split Military District, and the coordinator for sanitation. This was the only acceptable situation in military terms. We were all informed of it and all of us were privy to the elements that fell within our jurisdiction. Unfortunately, we were not aware of some other information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I'm looking at the clock. Are you about to finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: This is the last part. This is the last part about this particular issue. I just have a couple more questions on that so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you also know that we have to finish at 1.30. That's at least what we intend to do. So could you please put very focussed questions and not take more than three or four minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, do you specifically know what information was being sent to Dr. Brkic about what was happening with regard to the sanitation process in Knin in August 1995? Specifically.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I only know this from Mr. Gotovac, and anything else, when it comes to the mixed detachments, he did not receive any reports from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And very quickly, if we could look at item number 8 of General Cervenko' order, which is on the last -- or, sorry page 5 in English, which discusses the actual daily reporting required. And very specifically, Mr. Sruk, it indicates here that the reports are to be sent to the OPL, but moreover, that the OPL sector of the Croatian Army Main Staff is also supposed to forward reports of appropriate scope to the Ministry of Health -- or sorry, the Ministry of Defence Health Administration via regular channels. Can you explain that, because that seems to suggest that those reports -- or portions of the reports or appropriate scope are going to the Health Administration. Do you know anything specifically about what was contained in those reports to the Health Administration, of which Dr. Brkic was the chief?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: Just as I said before, the chain of events was such that us, as military, upon the orders of General Cervenko, were reporting to the OPLs of the Main Staff. Furthermore, General Gotovina did not have the authority to order OPL whom to forward these reports to. This was done by the Main Staff, and this is the usual way of reporting and the correct way of reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, Mr. Carrier put you to the paragraph 8 of this order by Mr. Cervenko, in which he instructs the OPL to forward reports of appropriate scope to the MORH Health Administration via regular channels. Have you ever seen such a report which was sent to the Health Administration of the Ministry of Defence? Have you ever seen such a report? A very factual question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not have seen them from my position. I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You never saw them. Do you have any specific knowledge of the content of those reports by other means than having looked at them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The part of the report that started from the coordination and went to the chief of the medical corps of the garrison, this is what I saw, of course. But furthermore, from there on, I could not have seen them, so I saw what came up to my level of -- in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That answers your question, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No more questions. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The document we're looking at, Exhibit D598, in this document, General Cervenko, Chief of the Main Staff, set out the procedure for sanitation -- sanitisation after Operation Oluja, and you've been directed to the contents of that, and, in particular, paragraph 7, where head of Health Services in the operations, logistics sector of the Main Staff were to coordinate, supervise, provide expert advice, and unclear issues to be resolved in coordination with the Ministry of Defence Health Administration. Considering, then, General Cervenko's order, as you have, was there any need for Dr. Brkic to have an order signed by General Cermak to carry out any duties?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not grasp your question, the last part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: General Cervenko set out here in his order of the 5th of August the procedure for sanitisation after Operation Oluja. He gave a coordination role to Brigadier Zlatar and Lieutenant Perajica and said unclear issues should be resolved in coordination with the Ministry of Defence Health Administration. Was there any need, considering General Cervenko's order, for Dr. Brkic to have an order from General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I just had one quick question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sruk, you were asked a question about these mixed sanitation unit and General Gotovina's order of the 11th of August and the fact that in point 1, the person identified would be an HV commander. In your experience as someone who worked in the logistics base, could General Gotovina subordinate HV personnel and logistics to the civilian government? In other words, could you have formally been subordinated to a civilian person to work, or would you always have to have someone in the HV supervising you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO SRUK
utterances.text: When any type of order was in question, it had to be issued by a soldier to a soldier and we carried out tasks as soldiers. I never experienced that my commander subordinated me to any civilian type of institution when there were other ways to do it. I have no such information, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Sruk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sruk, one question. Today, during your testimony when talking about what you saw in the hole upon arrival at the Knin cemetery you said: "And I have to say, when I recall these pictures today, I believe that they did it with the best of intentions." Now, what specifically in the picture made you believe that there were good intentions behind what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't customary to bury anybody in a pit, in a hole, but, rather, for dead bodies to be interred, a single individual body in one grave. Persons who started carrying out this sanitation in this unprofessional manner, nonetheless, they did not throw in these bodies but they laid them down in order, possibly believing that they did it properly. So they were not destroying anything. They did, in a way, inter them, so that I believe they are intentions were good. And it certainly was better even done this way, than if they had been left in the streets or wherever else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was just the one outstanding issue of the document I wanted to put in. But if we can't deal with it today, I understand, given time constraints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If can you deal with that in one or two questions, then please do so. Then even if we take three minutes more, then we'll have to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: It was just a matter of hoping to just put it in. I gave the number to my friends to look at so they'd have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you mean the tendering from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, just that one document. It's 65 ter 7452, which is basically the same as D30, D1060, D612 although it's to a different addressee, which is the issue, so it is slightly different. So that is the only change really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm told it is not a duplicate. It is another in the chain. No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. No objections from the other Defence counsel. Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2653.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. If there's no other matter -- Mr. Carrier, were you able to find the document to which P2652 is a correction?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: We haven't yet but I will try to update Your Honour tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it would have been preferred to have it here when the witness is still there, but if you didn't find it, then we will have to accept that for the time being. Mr. Sruk, this concludes your evidence in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I hope that you will have a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 28th of October, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom III.
